clinicalPearls: The Keith-Wagener-Barker classification grades severity from grade I through IV and correlates with systemic vascular risk
Grade I shows mild generalised arteriolar narrowing and grade II adds focal narrowing and arteriovenous nipping (Gunn sign; the related Salus sign is venous deflection at the crossing)
Grade III adds flame haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots and hard exudates, which may form a macular star
Grade IV (malignant or accelerated hypertension) adds optic disc swelling and is a medical emergency
Chronic arteriolosclerosis produces copper-wiring and later silver-wiring of the arterioles
Fundus findings are a window onto systemic end-organ damage and predict cerebrovascular and cardiac risk
Management is directed at controlled lowering of blood pressure and reduction of overall cardiovascular risk rather than any ocular intervention
reference.pathophysiology: Sustained elevation of blood pressure first causes reactive arteriolar vasoconstriction and then structural arteriolosclerosis with medial hyperplasia and intimal thickening. Breakdown of the inner blood-retinal barrier allows leakage that produces haemorrhages and hard exudates, while precapillary arteriolar occlusion causes ischaemic cotton-wool spots. In accelerated (malignant) hypertension, fibrinoid necrosis of arterioles and choroidal vascular compromise damage the optic nerve head, producing disc swelling that reflects a systemic hypertensive emergency.
additionalInvestigations: Blood pressure measurement, ideally repeated and including ambulatory monitoring where appropriate
Dilated fundus examination to grade the retinopathy
Fasting glucose or HbA1c to detect coexisting diabetes
Renal function tests and urinalysis for end-organ damage
Lipid profile and broader cardiovascular risk assessment
Optical coherence tomography if macular oedema or exudate threatens the fovea
redFlags: Grade IV changes with optic disc swelling indicating malignant hypertension
Very high blood pressure with headache, chest pain or breathlessness
Accompanying neurological symptoms suggesting hypertensive encephalopathy or stroke
Bilateral disc oedema requiring differentiation from raised intracranial pressure
reference.prognosis: Mild and moderate changes are largely reversible with sustained blood pressure control, whereas malignant hypertension is a life-threatening emergency with significant systemic morbidity and mortality if untreated.
pitfalls: Mistaking hypertensive disc swelling for primary papilloedema and missing the underlying blood pressure crisis
Failing to measure blood pressure in any patient with retinal vascular signs
Overlooking asymptomatic malignant hypertension detected first in the fundus
Not screening for coexisting diabetes when retinopathy is present
references: American Academy of Ophthalmology, Basic and Clinical Science Course: Retina and Vitreous
management: Control systemic blood pressure with antihypertensive therapy as the mainstay, which reverses mild to moderate changes
Treat malignant (grade IV) hypertension as an emergency with careful, controlled blood pressure reduction to avoid ischaemic optic and cerebral injury
Reduce overall cardiovascular risk with lipid-lowering therapy, glycaemic control and smoking cessation
Manage sight-threatening macular oedema or exudate encroaching on the fovea in liaison with ophthalmology
Investigate and treat secondary causes of hypertension and screen for coexisting diabetes
Monitor blood pressure, serial dilated fundus examination and renal function for end-organ damage
